stem: What is a pathogen?

options.content: Any microorganism
options.rationale: Most microorganisms are harmless or useful.

options.content: A disease-causing organism
options.rationale: Pathogens include some viruses, bacteria, fungi, protoctists and worms.

options.content: A chemical that kills bacteria
options.rationale: That describes an antibiotic or a disinfectant.

options.content: An animal that carries a disease from one host to another
options.rationale: That is a vector.

explanation: A pathogen is a disease-causing organism. Examples are the bacterium that causes cholera and the protoctist that causes malaria.

stem: What is a transmissible disease?

options.content: A disease caused by a lack of a nutrient in the diet, such as scurvy
options.rationale: That is a deficiency disease, which cannot be passed on.

options.content: A disease that is inherited from the parents through their genes
options.rationale: Inherited diseases are passed on in genes, not from host to host.

options.content: A disease whose pathogen can be passed from one host to another
options.rationale: For example cholera, malaria and tuberculosis.

options.content: A disease caused by the body wearing out with age, such as osteoarthritis
options.rationale: That is a degenerative disease.

explanation: A transmissible disease is one in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another, directly or indirectly.

stem: Match each disease with the way its pathogen is usually transmitted.

right.content: The bite of an infected female mosquito
Breathing in droplets from an infected person's cough
Blood and other body fluids, for example by sharing needles
Bacteria from soil entering a deep wound

explanation: Cholera spreads in water contaminated with faeces, malaria through mosquito bites, tuberculosis in airborne droplets and HIV through blood and other body fluids. Soil bacteria entering a wound cause tetanus, which is not listed.
hints: One of the routes on the right belongs to a disease that is not listed.

stem: True or false: acid in the stomach kills many of the pathogens swallowed with food and drink.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is a chemical defence against pathogens.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: the hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills many pathogens in food and drink.

explanation: The stomach makes hydrochloric acid, which kills many of the pathogens swallowed with food and drink. It is one of the body's chemical barriers.

stem: Which of these is an example of **indirect** transmission of a pathogen?

options.content: HIV passing from a mother to her baby during birth
options.rationale: This is direct transmission through body fluids.

options.content: Drinking water that is contaminated with faeces
options.rationale: The pathogen reaches the person through the water.

options.content: Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person
options.rationale: This is direct transmission through body fluids.

options.content: Touching the infected skin of a person with ringworm
options.rationale: This is direct contact with the infected person.

explanation: In indirect transmission the pathogen is carried by something else, such as water, food, surfaces, air or an animal. Drinking contaminated water is indirect; the other examples pass the pathogen straight from person to person.

stem: Select **all** the parts of the body that help to stop pathogens causing disease.

options.content: Red blood cells
options.rationale: Red blood cells carry oxygen; they do not fight pathogens.

options.content: The bladder
options.rationale: The bladder stores urine; it is not a defence against pathogens.

options.content: Hairs in the nose
options.rationale: They trap dust and pathogens.

options.content: Mucus in the airways
options.rationale: It traps pathogens, which are then removed.

options.content: Stomach acid
options.rationale: It kills many pathogens in food.

options.content: White blood cells
options.rationale: They engulf pathogens and make antibodies.

options.content: Insulin
options.rationale: Insulin is a hormone that lowers blood glucose.

options.content: Skin
options.rationale: A tough barrier that pathogens cannot cross unless it is damaged.

explanation: The body's defences include the skin and hairs in the nose (mechanical barriers), mucus and stomach acid (chemical barriers) and white blood cells. Red blood cells, insulin and the bladder have other jobs.

stem: How does a Blair ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine help to reduce the spread of disease?

options.content: Insecticide sprayed down the vent pipe kills the flies and mosquitoes breeding in the pit
options.rationale: There is no insecticide; the design itself traps flies.

options.content: Chlorine added to the pit kills the bacteria in the faeces, so flies pick up no pathogens
options.rationale: VIP latrines do not use chlorine.

options.content: It is built right next to the well, so people can wash their hands as soon as they come out
options.rationale: Latrines must be built well away from, and downhill of, water sources.

options.content: Flies are drawn to the light at the top of the screened vent pipe and trapped, so fewer reach food
options.rationale: The dark shelter and screened vent pipe trap flies.

explanation: Inside, the latrine is kept dark. Flies in the pit fly towards the light at the top of the vent pipe, where the fly screen traps them until they die. Fewer flies reach food carrying pathogens from faeces, and air moving up the pipe removes smells.
hints: Why does the vent pipe have a screen on top?

stem: How do houseflies spread diseases such as typhoid?

options.content: They carry bacteria on their feet and mouthparts from faeces to food
options.rationale: People then eat the contaminated food.

options.content: They inject bacteria into the blood when they bite people at night
options.rationale: Houseflies do not bite people.

options.content: They release poisons into the air that people then breathe in
options.rationale: Flies do not release poisons into the air.

options.content: They lay eggs in drinking water that hatch into bacteria
options.rationale: Fly eggs hatch into maggots, not bacteria.

explanation: Houseflies feed and breed on faeces and rotting refuse. Bacteria stick to their feet, bodies and mouthparts and are left on food they land on. Covering food and disposing of faeces and refuse safely reduces this spread.
hints: Where have the flies been before they land on food?

stem: Why is chlorine added to the water supplied to towns?

options.content: To improve the taste and smell of the water
options.rationale: Chlorine does not improve the taste.

options.content: To remove mud and soil particles from the water
options.rationale: Particles are removed by settling and filtering.

options.content: To kill pathogens such as bacteria in the water
options.rationale: This prevents diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

options.content: To add the mineral ions that the body needs
options.rationale: Chlorine is added to kill microorganisms, not to supply minerals.

explanation: Chlorine kills pathogens, such as the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid, so treated water is safe to drink.

stem: Which is the best description of **health**?

options.content: Not having any disease, injury or disability at the present time
options.rationale: Health is more than the absence of disease.

options.content: Being physically fit and strong enough to work and play sport
options.rationale: Physical fitness is only one part of health.

options.content: Having enough money for food, medicines and visits to a clinic
options.rationale: Money may help, but it is not what health means.

options.content: Complete physical, mental and social well-being
options.rationale: Health includes the mind and social life as well as the body, not just the absence of disease.

explanation: Health is a state of complete physical, mental (including emotional) and social well-being, and not simply the absence of disease or illness.

stem: Match each cause of disease with an example.

right.content: Skin cancer after many years of strong sunlight

explanation: Measles is caused by a virus; sickle-cell anaemia is inherited; kwashiorkor is caused by a lack of protein; ultraviolet radiation from the sun can cause skin cancer; osteoarthritis comes from joints wearing out. Lead poisoning is caused by a chemical, which is not one of the causes listed.
hints: Kwashiorkor is linked to a lack of protein in the diet.

stem: Select **all** the non-infectious diseases.

options.content: Kwashiorkor
options.rationale: A deficiency disease caused by too little protein.

options.content: Typhoid
options.rationale: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium and is infectious.

options.content: Malaria
options.rationale: Malaria is caused by a protoctist and is spread by mosquitoes.

options.content: Haemophilia
options.rationale: An inherited (genetic) disease in which blood does not clot properly.

options.content: Scurvy
options.rationale: A deficiency disease caused by too little vitamin C.

options.content: Influenza
options.rationale: Influenza is caused by a virus and is infectious.

options.content: Skin cancer
options.rationale: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division; it cannot be caught.

explanation: Non-infectious diseases cannot be passed from person to person: deficiency diseases (kwashiorkor, scurvy), genetic diseases (haemophilia) and cancer. Influenza, malaria and typhoid are caused by pathogens and are infectious.
hints: Ask: is it caused by a pathogen that can be passed on?

stem: True or false: cancer is an infectious disease that can be caught by touching a person who has it.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so. Cancer is a non-infectious disease caused by uncontrolled cell division; it cannot be caught.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Cancer is non-infectious: it develops when cells divide uncontrollably.

explanation: Cancer is a non-infectious disease. Cells divide uncontrollably and form a tumour; it cannot be passed on by touch.

stem: Which practice at a school tuck-shop best reduces the risk of spreading disease through food?

options.content: Keeping raw and cooked meat on the same plate
options.rationale: Bacteria from raw meat can contaminate the cooked meat.

options.content: Wiping hands on an apron instead of washing them
options.rationale: This does not remove pathogens from the hands.

options.content: Leaving cooked food uncovered to cool all day
options.rationale: Flies can land on it and bacteria can multiply in warm food.

options.content: Cooking meat thoroughly and keeping cooked food covered
options.rationale: Heat kills pathogens, and covers keep flies off.

explanation: Thorough cooking kills pathogens, and covering cooked food keeps flies off it. Raw and cooked food should be kept apart and hands washed with soap.
hints: Which option both kills pathogens and stops new ones arriving?

stem: A town treats its sewage before releasing the water into a river. Why does this reduce disease in villages downstream?

options.content: Pathogens from faeces are killed or removed, so the river water is less contaminated
options.rationale: Fewer pathogens reach drinking and washing water.

options.content: Treated sewage adds chlorine to the river, which protects people from all diseases
options.rationale: Sewage treatment does not protect people against all diseases.

options.content: Treated water makes the river flow faster, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it
options.rationale: Sewage treatment does not change the speed of the river.

options.content: Treatment removes the fish and snails from the river, which carry many diseases
options.rationale: Sewage treatment does not remove fish or snails; it removes pathogens from faeces.

explanation: Untreated sewage contains pathogens from human faeces, such as cholera and typhoid bacteria. Treatment kills or removes them, so water taken from the river downstream is far less likely to spread disease.

stem: After heavy rain, several families in a village fall ill with diarrhoea. They all collect drinking water from a shallow, unprotected well that is a short distance downhill from a pit latrine.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the most likely way the pathogens reached the families?

options.content: Mosquitoes that bred in the rainwater bit the families at night
options.rationale: Diarrhoeal diseases are not spread by mosquitoes.

options.content: Rain washed faeces from the latrine area into the well, contaminating the water
options.rationale: Faeces from the latrine reached the water supply.

options.content: The pathogens were breathed in from the coughs of people in the village
options.rationale: Coughing spreads airborne diseases such as TB, not diarrhoea.

options.content: The families shook hands with visitors who had come from another village
options.rationale: Contaminated water is a far more likely source when several families who share a well are ill.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways the families could make their drinking water safe.

points.description: One method, e.g. boil the water
A second method, e.g. add chlorine / water treatment tablets; use water from a protected borehole or treated supply; store water in clean, covered containers

parts.explanation: For example, boil the water before drinking it, or treat it with chlorine tablets; collect water from a protected borehole and store it in a clean, covered container.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why washing hands with soap at a tippy-tap after using the latrine reduces the spread of disease.

points.description: Soap and water remove pathogens (from faeces) from the hands
So the pathogens are not passed to food, to the mouth or to other people

parts.explanation: Washing with soap removes pathogens from faeces on the hands, so they are not passed on to food, to the mouth or to other people.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Where should the village build a new latrine?

options.content: Right next to the well, so it is easy to reach
options.rationale: Faeces could seep into the well.

options.content: Uphill from the well
options.rationale: Rainwater and seepage would flow from the latrine towards the well.

options.content: Downhill from the well and well away from it
options.rationale: Water from the latrine area cannot then flow into the well.

options.content: In the dry bed of a stream
options.rationale: Water would wash the faeces downstream when the stream flows.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Is the spread of pathogens in contaminated water direct or indirect transmission?

rejected.feedback: The pathogens reach people through the water, so the transmission is indirect.
The pathogens reach people through the water, so the transmission is indirect.

explanation: The rain washed faeces from the latrine area into the shallow well, so the families drank water containing pathogens: indirect transmission. Boiling or chlorinating water, using protected boreholes, washing hands with soap and siting latrines downhill and well away from water sources all break the chain.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Contaminated drinking water from the well.

**(b)** For example, boiling; chlorine tablets; a protected borehole; clean covered storage.

**(c)** Soap removes pathogens from the hands, so they are not passed to food, mouths or other people.

**(d)** Downhill from the well and well away from it.

**(e)** Indirect.
hints: Think about where the rainwater flowed.

stem:
A school health club put up identical sticky fly traps for one week at four places around the school.

| Place | Number of flies caught |
| --- | --- |
| Next to an open refuse pit | 86 |
| Next to refuse bins with lids | 14 |
| Inside the shelter of a Blair VIP latrine | 9 |
| In the kitchen, where food is kept covered | 5 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of flies caught next to the bins with lids, compared with the open refuse pit. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why an open refuse pit increases the risk of disease at the school.

points.description: Rotting refuse attracts flies, which feed and breed (lay eggs) there
Flies then carry pathogens from the refuse to food, which people eat

parts.explanation: Flies feed and breed on the rotting refuse, then carry pathogens on their bodies to food that people eat.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why did the club use identical traps at every place?

options.content: So that more flies would be caught in total at each place
options.rationale: Identical traps do not increase the catch.

options.content: So that only the place changed, making it a fair test
options.rationale: Different traps could catch flies differently.

options.content: Because flies are only attracted to traps that look the same
options.rationale: Flies do not respond to whether traps match.

options.content: So that all the flies in the school would be killed in one week
options.rationale: The aim was to compare places, not to kill every fly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest how the club could make its results more reliable.

points.description: Repeat for more weeks / use several traps at each place and calculate a mean

parts.explanation: Put several traps at each place, or repeat the count for several weeks, and calculate mean numbers.

explanation: The reduction is 86 − 14 = 72 flies, which is 72 ÷ 86 × 100 = 83.7% of the number at the open pit. Uncovered refuse lets flies breed and pick up pathogens, which they carry to food; bins with lids, VIP latrines and covered food all reduce fly numbers.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Reduction $= 86 - 14 = 72$ flies. Percentage reduction $= \dfrac{72}{86} \times 100 = 83.72\ldots = 83.7\%$ (3 s.f.).

**(b)** Flies feed and breed on refuse, then carry pathogens to food.

**(c)** So that only the place changes: a fair test.

**(d)** More traps per place or more weeks; calculate means.

stem: Explain how each of the following helps to control the spread of disease: a clean water supply, hygienic food preparation, good personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment. [6]

points.description: Clean water supply: water is treated (filtered and chlorinated) or taken from protected boreholes, so waterborne pathogens (e.g. cholera, typhoid bacteria) are killed or kept out
Hygienic food preparation: thorough cooking kills pathogens; covering food keeps flies off; keeping raw and cooked food apart prevents contamination
Personal hygiene: washing hands with soap (after the toilet, before handling food) removes pathogens
Personal hygiene: covering coughs and sneezes reduces the spread of droplets
Waste disposal: refuse is collected, covered, buried or burned, so flies, rats and mosquitoes (vectors) cannot feed or breed in it
Sewage treatment kills / removes pathogens from faeces before water is returned to rivers; toilets keep faeces away from water and food
Overall, fewer pathogens reach people / the chain of transmission is broken

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A **clean water supply** is filtered and chlorinated, or comes from protected boreholes, so pathogens such as cholera and typhoid bacteria are killed or kept out of drinking water. In **hygienic food preparation**, thorough cooking kills pathogens, covering food keeps flies off it and raw meat is kept away from cooked food. Good **personal hygiene**, especially washing hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food, removes pathogens from the hands, and covering coughs reduces droplets. **Waste disposal** in covered bins, or by burying or burning refuse, removes places where flies, rats and mosquitoes feed and breed. **Sewage treatment** kills or removes pathogens from faeces before the water returns to rivers. Each measure stops pathogens reaching people, breaking the chain of transmission.

explanation: For each measure, say what it does and how that stops pathogens reaching people.
hints: For each measure: what does it remove or kill, and how does that stop transmission?

stem: Patients with severe burns are at a high risk of infection. Which is the best explanation?

options.content: The skin, which is normally a barrier to pathogens, has been destroyed
options.rationale: The mechanical barrier is broken.

options.content: Burns increase the acid in the stomach, which lets pathogens into the blood
options.rationale: Stomach acid kills pathogens; burns do not make infection more likely this way.

options.content: Burns stop the hairs in the nose trapping dust, so pathogens are breathed in
options.rationale: The nose is not the main problem in a burn.

options.content: Burned skin cells turn into bacteria, which then spread through the body
options.rationale: Pathogens come from the surroundings; the damaged skin lets them in.

explanation: Intact skin is a tough mechanical barrier. A severe burn destroys it over a large area, so bacteria and fungi from the surroundings can enter the body. Burns are therefore kept very clean and covered.
hints: Which defence normally covers the whole body?

stem: Name the type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.

rejected.feedback: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Cells that engulf pathogens are phagocytes.
Lymphocytes make antibodies. Cells that engulf pathogens are phagocytes.

explanation: Phagocytes engulf pathogens and digest them with enzymes; this is called phagocytosis. Lymphocytes, another type of white blood cell, make antibodies.

stem: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?

options.content: Cholera
options.rationale: Cholera is caused by a bacterium.

options.content: Malaria
options.rationale: Malaria is caused by a protoctist, Plasmodium.

options.content: Measles
options.rationale: Measles is caused by a virus.

options.content: Bilharzia
options.rationale: Bilharzia is caused by a parasitic worm, Schistosoma.

explanation: Measles is caused by a virus. Cholera is bacterial, malaria is caused by the protoctist Plasmodium, and bilharzia by the blood fluke Schistosoma.

stem: What is the general name for an organism, such as a mosquito, that carries a pathogen from one host to another?

rejected.feedback: The host is the organism the pathogen lives in. The carrier between hosts is a vector.
The pathogen is the organism that causes the disease; the mosquito carries it.
The parasite (pathogen) is carried by the vector.

explanation: A vector carries a pathogen from one host to another. Female Anopheles mosquitoes are the vectors of malaria.
